F145.r: Warm-season (C4) grasses like bermudagrass and bahiagrass grow fast in heat but make more fiber and less protein than cool-season grasses like fescue, orchardgrass or wheat pasture. That's why stockers gain much more on wheat pasture than on summer bermuda.
F145.1.0: On good warm-season pasture a stocker gains about 1 to 1.5 lb a day; on wheat pasture, 2 to 2.5 lb.
F145.1.1: With supplement on summer grass it can reach about 1.8 to 2.2 lb.
F145.1.2: In the feedyard on a finishing ration it can gain 3.5 to 4 lb.
F145.2.1: Supplement protein on dormant winter range and energy on lush spring grass when you want more gain.
F145.2.2: Legumes like alfalfa and clovers raise pasture protein.
F149.1.1: The Brazilian BR-CORTE tables were built with Nelore and crosses, useful for Brahman-influenced cattle in the southern US.
F149.1.2: The US NASEM tables were built mainly with British and Continental breeds, the typical feedyard cattle.
F149.2.0: A 775 lb steer gaining 2.2 lb a day eats about 18 to 20 lb of dry matter.
F149.3.0: Rumi's calculators use values from these tables adjusted to your cattle type and climate. See Rumi, Feeding, Requirements by breed and climate.

F211.r: Crossing breeds adds hybrid vigor: more growth, fertility and survival than either parent. In the US most feeder cattle are British or British × Continental crosses, with Brahman crosses in the Gulf Coast and a fast-growing share of beef-on-dairy calves.

p: Angus × Hereford (black baldy): hardy, fertile and good at grading.
British × Continental (Charolais, Simmental, Limousin): more muscle and yield.
Brahman × British (Brangus, Braford, F1 tigerstripe) in hot, humid southern states.
Angus or other beef sires on Holstein and Jersey cows.
The calves grow and grade much better than straight dairy steers.
They're now a significant share of US fed cattle.
Uniform, black-hided British crosses usually bring the best feeder prices and fit Angus programs.
In the South, some Brahman influence helps cattle handle heat before they reach the yard.

F213.r: Some US breeds descend from the cattle brought by the Spanish five centuries ago. They adapted to heat, poor forage and insects and carry valuable genes.

p: Texas Longhorn: hardy, long-lived and easy calving.
Florida Cracker and Pineywoods: small, heat- and insect-tolerant Gulf Coast cattle.
Senepol (from the Caribbean), used in the Gulf Coast for heat tolerance.
Romosinuano, studied by USDA researchers in Florida.
Heat tolerance without Brahman: several carry the slick hair gene.
Good fertility and calm temperament.
More tender beef than Brahman.
Crossed with British breeds they add hybrid vigor and heat tolerance.
Straight heritage cattle are usually discounted as feeders: price them carefully.

F226.r: Zebu cattle (Bos indicus) include several breeds, each with its strengths. In the US, Brahman and its crosses are common in Texas, Florida and the Gulf Coast.
F226.3.0: Brahman-cross feeders from the South perform well, but feedyards and buyers often discount high-percentage Brahman cattle for tenderness and temperament.

F276.r: In the US the feedyard pays for growth, feed efficiency and grading. Black-hided British cattle and their crosses dominate, with Continental crosses, Holstein steers and beef-on-dairy cattle filling the rest.

p: Angus and Red Angus, Hereford, Shorthorn.
Good marbling and grading; Angus-type cattle can qualify for Certified Angus Beef.
Most US feeder cattle are black-hided.
Charolais, Simmental, Limousin, Gelbvieh.
More muscle, yield and growth; used in crosses with British breeds.
Brangus, Braford, Beefmaster, Santa Gertrudis, Simbrah.
Heat and insect tolerance; common from Texas to Florida.
Heavier Brahman influence can reduce tenderness and grading.
Holstein steers: very uniform, long feeding period, lower dressing.
Beef-on-dairy crosses grow and grade much better than straight Holsteins.
Record each animal's breed when you create the lot.
Compare gain and margin by breed with your own numbers. Also see Guide, Reference tables, Breeds for feeding.
